source_text:
Gal 2,18 Πρὸς τὸν
Πέτρον ὁ λόγος· σὺ κατέλυσας αὐτὰ δόγματι ὅπερ ἀπεστάλη παρ' ὑμῶν τοῖς
Ἀντιοχεῦσι καὶ πάσῃ τῇ οἰκουμένῃ. ἀπρεπὲς οὖν ταύτα διδάσκειν ἑτέρους, ὧν τῆς
ἐπιμελείας ἀπέστης καὶ ἰδίῳ κατέλυσας δόγματι. Gal 2,19– Ὁ νόμος τῶν σωματικῶν
ἔχει τὴν ἐργασίαν καὶ τὴν ἀπόλαυσιν, τόδε φάγε καὶ τόδε μὴ φάγῃς, σάββατον
τήρησον, περιτομήν. ἡ χάρις οὐ βούλεταί σε διὰ τούτων εὐδοκιμεῖν. ἐνεκρώθην οὖν,
φησί, τούτοις. τί χρείαν ἔχω νόμου; Ζῶ δὲ οὐκέτι ἐγώ, ζῇ δὲ ἐν ἐμοὶ Χριστός. ὃ ἐγὼ
ἔζων ἐμαυτῷ, ὑπὸ νόμον ἤμην. ἐπειδὴ δὲ Χριστὸς ζῇ ἐν ἐμοί, ὁ μηκέτι ὑπὸ νόμον
ἀλλ' ἐν οὐρανοῖς ἐκ δεξιῶν τοῦ πατρός, οὐκ ἀθετῶ τὸν ἐν ἐμοὶ ζῶντα. Ὃ δὲ νῦν ζῶ
ἐν σαρκί, ἐν πίστει ζῶ. πιστεύω γὰρ εἰς τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ θεοῦ. εἰ δὲ ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ ᾧ
πιστεύω, ἐν δεξιᾷ τοῦ πατρός, ἐν οὐρανοῖς πολιτεύομαι· ὁ δὲ νόμος ἐν τοῖς ἐπὶ γῆς
εἶχε τὰς τηρήσεις. οὐκ ἄρα ὑπόκειμαι νόμῳ. 301 Gal 3,19–22 Ἐβάρει πλέον ὁ νόμος,
καὶ διακονία θανάτου διὰ τοῦτο ὠνόμασται. πῶς οὖν τῶν παραβάσεων χάριν
προσετέθη, φησίν; ἐν συντόμῳ ῥήματι τοιοῦτόν ἐστιν· πρὸ νόμου καὶ ὁ νοῦς τῶν
ἀνθρώπων μετὰ τῆς σαρκὸς ἐδούλευσε τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ καὶ ἔστεργε τὸ κακόν, δοθέντος
τοῦ νόμου ὁ μὲν νοῦς ἐπαιδεύθη, ἡ δὲ σὰρξ ἔτι κατείχετο. ἐπεὶ οὖν ὁ μὲν ἀγνοῶν τὴν
ἁμαρτίαν ὅτι ἁμαρτία ἦν, τὴν ἀσέβειαν ὡς εὐσέβειαν μετιὼν καὶ σπουδαιότερον
αὐτῇ προσέχει, ὁ δὲ γνοὺς ὅτι κακόν, τοῦτο γοῦν κερδανεῖ τὸ συνειδέναι ὅτι
παραβαίνει, καὶ ἐπιθυμεῖ τῷ θεῷ ὑπακοῦσαι. διὰ τοῦτο ἐδόθη νόμος ὁ δυνάμενος
ζωοποιῆσαι, ἀντὶ τοῦ εἰ ἐδόθη νόμος, οὐκ ἐδόθη, φησί, κατὰ τῶν ἐπαγγελιῶν τοῦ
θεοῦ, ἀλλ' οὐδὲ διὰ παντὸς κρατεῖν ἐδύνατο. Gal 3,23 Εἰ καὶ μηδὲν ἕτερον κατώρθου
ὁ νόμος, ἀλλὰ τὸ τὸν θεὸν εἰδέναι παρεῖχεν. τὸ δὲ τὸν θεὸν εἰδέναι ἕτοιμον ἐποίει
πρὸς τὴν τῆς χάριτος ὑποδοχήν. Gal 3,27–28 Οὐχ ἡ τοῦ νόμου τήρησις, φησί,
βελτίονας ποιεῖ τοὺς πιστεύσαντας τῶν ἀπὸ τῶν ἐθνῶν τοὺς Ἰουδαίους, ἀλλ' ἡ
δύναμις τοῦ βαπτίσματος τὸ Χριστὸν ἐνδύσασθαι παρέχουσα, κοινὴν ποιεῖ τὴν χάριν
πάντων ὁμοῦ, βαρβάρων, Ἑλλήνων, Ἰουδαίων, θήλεος, ἄρρενος. οὐχ ἁπλῶς δὲ
παρέμιξε τὸ θῆλυ καὶ τὸ ἄρρεν–ὅσον γὰρ εἷς τῷ ῥήματι ἐζήτει πρὸς τὸ προκείμενον–,
ἀλλ' εἰ τὸ ἄρρεν καὶ τὸ θῆλυ διαφέρον εἰς μίαν χάριν συνάγει τὸ βάπτισμα, πόσῳ
μᾶλλον Ἕλληνα καὶ Ἰουδαῖον. Gal 4,8–10 Νῦν βούλεται δεῖξαι ὅτι μετὰ τὸ τὴν χάριν
ἐλθεῖν, κἂν δοκῇ τις κατὰ νόμον σάββατον τηρεῖν καὶ νεομηνίας καὶ ἑορτάς, ὥσπερ
εἰδωλολατρεῖ τοῖς στοιχείοις οἷς ἐθρήσκευεν ἐθνικὸς ὤν, ἄλλως δουλεύων.
thought_title: Dead to law and made one by baptism
orientation: Severianus presents Paul rebuking Peter and arguing that law was a temporary bodily discipline while grace and baptism free Jews and Gentiles alike.
pass_a_gloss: The word is to Peter: you tore these down by a decree which was sent out from you to the Antiochians and to the whole inhabited world. It is therefore unfitting to teach others these things, from the care of which you stood away and which you tore down by your own decree. The law has the working and the enjoyment of bodily things: eat this and do not eat this, keep sabbath, circumcision. Grace does not want you to gain approval through these things. I have been put to death therefore to these things, he says. What need of law do I have? But I no longer live, but Christ lives in me. What I was living for myself, I was under law. But since Christ lives in me, who is no longer under law but in the heavens at the right of the Father, I do not set aside the one living in me. But what I now live in flesh, in faith I live. For I have faith in the Son of God. But if the Son of God in whom I have faith is at the right of the Father, I am a citizen in the heavens; but the law had its observances among the things upon earth. Therefore I am not subject to law. Law weighed still heavier, and for this reason was named service of death. How then was it added for the sake of transgressions, he says? In a short saying it is such: before law both the mind of men with the flesh was enslaved to sin and loved the evil, and when law was given the mind was trained, but the flesh was still held down. Since then the one who did not know sin that it was sin pursues impiety as piety and attends to it more earnestly, but the one who knew that it is evil will gain this at least, to know together that he transgresses, and he desires to obey God. For this reason law was given that was able to give life, instead of saying if law was given, it was not given against the promises of God, he says, but neither was it able to hold sway through all time. Even if law accomplished nothing else, yet it furnished knowing God. But knowing God made one ready for the reception of grace. Not the observance of law, he says, makes the Jews who have faith better than those from the nations who have faith, but the power of baptism which furnishes putting on Christ makes the grace common of all together, barbarians, Greeks, Jews, female, male. But he did not simply mix the female and the male — for as much as one sought by the phrase for the matter lying before — but if baptism gathers the male and the female which differ into one grace, how much more Greek and Jew. Now he wants to show that after grace came, even if someone seems to keep sabbath according to law and new moons and feasts, as though he practices idolatry with the elemental things which he used to worship when being one of the nations, while serving in a different way.

pass_b_english: Severianus says Paul directs his words to Peter. You annulled them, he says, by a decree, the same decree that was sent out from you to the people in Antioch and to the whole world. It is unfitting, then, to teach others the things whose care you abandoned and which you annulled by your own decree.

The law, Paul argues, holds the working and the enjoyment of bodily things: eat this and do not eat that, keep the Sabbath, circumcision. Grace does not want you to gain approval through these. So Paul says, I died to these things. What need do I have of law? I no longer live, but Christ lives in me (Galatians 2:20). What I lived for myself, I was under law. But since Christ lives in me, and he is no longer under law but in heaven at the right hand of the Father, I do not set aside the one who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh, I live in faith (Galatians 2:20). For I have faith in the Son of God. If the Son of God in whom I have faith is at the right hand of the Father, then I am a citizen in heaven. The law kept its observances among things on earth. So I am not subject to law.

The law weighed heavily, and for that reason it was called a service of death. How then was it "added because of transgressions," as Paul says (Galatians 3:19)? In a brief word it is this. Before law, the mind of human beings served sin together with the flesh and loved evil. When law was given, the mind was taught, but the flesh was still held fast. The one who did not know that sin was sin pursued impiety as if it were piety and gave himself to it more eagerly. The one who knew that it was evil gained at least this, that he knew he was transgressing, and he desired to obey God. Therefore "a law was given that could give life" (Galatians 3:21)—meaning "if a law had been given." It was not given, he says, against the promises of God, yet neither could it prevail forever.
Even if law accomplished nothing else, it gave knowledge of God. And knowledge of God made them ready to receive grace.

Keeping the law, Paul says, does not make Jewish believers better than believers from the nations. The power of baptism, which grants them to be clothed in Christ, makes the grace of all together common, barbarians, Greeks, Jews, female, male. He did not merely mix female and male together, for he sought by that word only what served his present point, but his meaning is that if baptism gathers male and female, though they differ, into one grace, how much more does it gather Greek and Jew.

Now he wants to show that after grace has come, even if someone keeps Sabbath and new moons and feasts according to law, he is as though he practices idolatry with the elemental things which he worshipped when he was a pagan, serving only in a different way.
notes: 301 is a printed page number in the source and is not translated

problems.quote: For this reason law was given that was able to give life (Galatians 3:21), instead of saying that if law was given, it was not given against the promises of God, but neither was it able to prevail forever.
problems.source_quote: διὰ τοῦτο ἐδόθη νόμος ὁ δυνάμενος ζωοποιῆσαι, ἀντὶ τοῦ εἰ ἐδόθη νόμος, οὐκ ἐδόθη, φησί, κατὰ τῶν ἐπαγγελιῶν τοῦ θεοῦ, ἀλλ' οὐδὲ διὰ παντὸς κρατεῖν ἐδύνατο.
problems.why: Misconstrues the gloss "instead of 'if a law had been given'" by merging the following main clause into it, garbling Paul's claim and dropping "he says."
problems.fix: Therefore "a law was given that could give life" (Galatians 3:21)—meaning "if a law had been given." It was not given, he says, against the promises of God, yet neither could it prevail forever.

problems.quote: instead of saying that if law was given, it was not given against the promises of God
problems.source_quote: ἀντὶ τοῦ εἰ ἐδόθη νόμος, οὐκ ἐδόθη, φησί, κατὰ τῶν ἐπαγγελιῶν τοῦ θεοῦ
problems.why: Clause structure contradicts itself; readers cannot tell what Paul affirms about the promises.
problems.fix: Paul says law was not given against God’s promises, answering the "if law was given" line in Galatians 3:21.
problems.ruling: English folds 'οὐκ ἐδόθη, φησί, κατὰ τῶν ἐπαγγελιῶν τοῦ θεοῦ' under 'instead of' ('ἀντὶ τοῦ') and drops 'φησί', garbling Paul's main clause.

problems.quote: How then, Paul says, was it added because of transgressions (Galatians 3:19)?
problems.source_quote: πῶς οὖν τῶν παραβάσεων χάριν προσετέθη, φησίν;
problems.why: Attributes the question "How then...?" to Paul, whereas Paul asserted "it was added because of transgressions" and the question is Severianus's or an objector's.
problems.fix: How then was it "added because of transgressions," as Paul says (Galatians 3:19)?
problems.ruling: πῶς…προσετέθη, φησίν makes Paul the asker; Gal 3:19 asserts addition for transgressions, not this how-question.

edits.old: How then, Paul says, was it added because of transgressions (Galatians 3:19)?
edits.new: How then was it "added because of transgressions," as Paul says (Galatians 3:19)?

edits.old: For this reason law was given that was able to give life (Galatians 3:21), instead of saying that if law was given, it was not given against the promises of God, but neither was it able to prevail forever.
edits.new: Therefore "a law was given that could give life" (Galatians 3:21)—meaning "if a law had been given." It was not given, he says, against the promises of God, yet neither could it prevail forever.

fixed: mistranslation fixed: ἀντὶ τοῦ εἰ ἐδόθη νόμος qualifies only the quotation ὁ δυνάμενος ζωοποιῆσαι, while οὐκ ἐδόθη...κατὰ τῶν ἐπαγγελιῶν is the separate main claim with φησί.
unreadable fixed by same edit: separated the 'if a law had been given' gloss from 'it was not given against the promises of God' so Paul's affirmation is clear.
speaker fixed: πῶς οὖν τῶν παραβάσεων χάριν προσετέθη, φησίν quotes Paul's assertion, while the πῶς question is Severianus's, so 'as Paul says' now modifies only the quotation.

last_rejected.quote: He did not merely mix female and male together, for he sought by that word only what served his present point
last_rejected.source_quote: οὐχ ἁπλῶς δὲ παρέμιξε τὸ θῆλυ καὶ τὸ ἄρρεν–ὅσον γὰρ εἷς τῷ ῥήματι ἐζήτει πρὸς τὸ προκείμενον–
last_rejected.why: οὐχ ἁπλῶς means 'not casually' (not 'not merely'), παρέμιξε means 'added in,' and the parenthesis voices a question about relevance rather than saying Paul sought 'only' what fit.
last_rejected.fix: He did not casually bring in female and male—for one might ask how that phrase bore on the matter at hand—
last_rejected.ruling: οὐχ ἁπλῶς, παρέμιξε, and ὅσον…προκείμενον sit within normal range; English keeps Paul’s limited rhetorical use, not casual mixing, for the baptism argument.
